course.title: Abnormal Psychology
course.description: Abnormal psychology studies patterns of thought, emotion, and behavior that cause distress or impairment, and the humane, evidence-based ways we come to understand and treat them. This course surveys how psychologists define abnormality, the major explanatory models and the DSM-5 classification system, and the main categories of disorder from anxiety and mood to psychosis, drawing on the overview article from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia. Throughout, the aim is accuracy and compassion: mental disorders are common, treatable, and nothing to be ashamed of.

questions.prompt: Clinicians often judge behavior as abnormal using several criteria together. Which set is a common shorthand for them?
questions.explanation: The 'four Ds' - distress, dysfunction, deviance, and danger - are a widely taught starting point, though none alone is decisive. See 'Defining abnormality and the history of treatment'.

questions.prompt: The large-scale movement in the mid-20th century to move patients out of long-stay mental hospitals into community care is called...
questions.explanation: Deinstitutionalization was enabled partly by new medications and shifting policy. See the history reading.

questions.prompt: The model that explains a disorder as the joint product of biological, psychological, and social factors is the...
questions.explanation: The biopsychosocial model, associated with George Engel, integrates several levels of explanation. See 'Models of psychopathology'.

questions.prompt: In the United States, the standard manual used to classify mental disorders is the...
questions.explanation: The DSM-5 is published by the American Psychiatric Association; the WHO publishes the ICD. See 'Classification and the DSM-5'.

questions.prompt: Obsessions are unwanted, intrusive thoughts; compulsions are the repetitive acts done to relieve them. Together they are the core of...
questions.explanation: OCD pairs obsessions with compulsions; exposure and response prevention is a leading treatment. See 'Anxiety, OCD, and trauma-related disorders'.

questions.prompt: A mood disorder marked by alternating episodes of depression and mania or hypomania is...
questions.explanation: Bipolar disorder involves mood episodes at both extremes; mood stabilizers such as lithium are often used. See 'Mood disorders, bipolar, and suicide risk'.

questions.prompt: Hallucinations and delusions in schizophrenia are usually grouped as...
questions.explanation: Positive symptoms add experiences (hallucinations, delusions); negative symptoms are reductions, such as flat affect. See 'Schizophrenia and other major disorders'.

questions.prompt: Which statement about mental illness is best supported by the evidence?
options: Disorders are rare and almost never treatable
Disorders are common and many respond well to treatment
Talking about disorders makes them worse
questions.explanation: Mental disorders are common and frequently treatable with therapy, medication, or both; stigma is a barrier, not a fact. See 'Approaches to treatment and reducing stigma'.

lessons.title: Defining abnormality and the history of treatment

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to explain why abnormality is hard to define with a single rule, and describe the common criteria clinicians use together. You will also be able to sketch how societies have cared for people with mental illness over time, from early asylums through the reform known as moral treatment to the 20th-century shift called deinstitutionalization. Warm-up from the diagnostic: name one reason a fixed, universal definition of abnormal behavior is difficult to pin down. As you read, keep a compassionate frame in mind. The people behind every category and statistic are ordinary human beings, and the history of this field is in part a history of learning to treat them with dignity rather than fear. By the end you should be able to say what distress, dysfunction, deviance, and danger each contribute to a judgment, and why no one of them is sufficient on its own.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Abnormal psychology studies patterns of thought, feeling, and behavior that depart from what a person's community expects and that cause problems for the person or those around them. Because cultures and situations vary, there is no single test for abnormality. Instead, clinicians weigh several signs together, often summarized as the four Ds: distress (the person suffers), dysfunction (daily life is impaired), deviance (behavior is far outside cultural norms), and danger (risk to self or others). Each has limits. Grief brings distress yet is not a disorder; a harmless eccentric may be deviant without being ill. Context matters enormously, so the same behavior can be healthy in one setting and a symptom in another. Historically, explanations swung between supernatural, biological, and psychological accounts. Treatment moved from confinement in crowded asylums toward more humane care, and later toward community-based services, though progress has been uneven and incomplete.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Several reformers shaped humane care. In France, Philippe Pinel is remembered for removing the chains from patients at the Bicetre and Salpetriere hospitals and arguing for calm, respectful treatment. In England, William Tuke founded the York Retreat, a model of what became known as moral treatment, which emphasized routine, kindness, and meaningful activity rather than restraint. In the United States, Dorothea Dix campaigned tirelessly for state hospitals and better conditions for people who were then confined in jails and poorhouses. In the 20th century, the arrival of medications such as chlorpromazine, together with changing law and policy, enabled deinstitutionalization, the large-scale move of patients from long-stay hospitals into community settings. The intent was greater freedom and dignity, but without adequate funding for community services many people were left without support, a gap that still shapes debates today. The broader classification tradition, which later reforms refined, owes much to systematic observers of symptoms over time.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check your answers. 1) Which of the four Ds refers to impaired daily functioning? 2) Give one reason distress alone does not prove a disorder. 3) Name the reformer linked with unchaining patients in Paris. 4) What was the aim of moral treatment? 5) What unintended problem followed deinstitutionalization when community services were underfunded? Answers: 1) Dysfunction. 2) Ordinary grief or stress can cause real distress without being a disorder, so distress must be weighed with other signs and context. 3) Philippe Pinel. 4) To replace restraint and fear with routine, kindness, respect, and purposeful activity. 5) Many people left hospitals but could not find adequate housing, treatment, or support in the community, leading to homelessness and untreated illness for some.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: A common mistake is treating any one criterion as proof of a disorder; abnormality is a judgment made from several signs plus context, not a single switch. Another mistake is reading history as a simple march of progress; care has advanced but also stumbled, and good intentions sometimes produced harm. A third is using stigmatizing language. Prefer person-first phrasing, such as a person with schizophrenia rather than a schizophrenic. Exit ticket: (a) List the four Ds. (b) Name one reformer and the change they are known for. Answers: (a) Distress, dysfunction, deviance, and danger. (b) For example, Dorothea Dix, known for campaigning to build and improve state hospitals in the United States, or Philippe Pinel, known for freeing patients from chains and promoting humane treatment.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to describe the main models psychologists use to explain mental disorder - biological, psychological, and sociocultural - and explain why most clinicians combine them in a biopsychosocial approach. You will be able to match each model to the kind of evidence it emphasizes and the kind of treatment it suggests. Warm-up from the diagnostic: which single model would you expect to point toward medication, and which toward talking therapy? As you read, notice that these models are lenses, not rivals fighting to the death. A single person's depression might involve inherited vulnerability, a habit of harsh self-criticism, and a stretch of isolation all at once. Holding several lenses at the same time is a mark of careful clinical thinking, and it keeps us from reducing a whole person to one cause.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The biological model locates disorder in the body: genes, brain structure, and chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. It suggests treatments such as medication. The psychological model covers several schools. The psychodynamic tradition traces symptoms to unconscious conflict and early experience. Behaviorism explains them through learning, where responses are conditioned by reward, punishment, and association. The cognitive approach focuses on thoughts and beliefs, arguing that distorted thinking fuels distress; the humanistic approach emphasizes growth, meaning, and self-acceptance. The sociocultural model widens the frame to family, poverty, discrimination, and culture, noting that stressful environments raise risk and that what counts as a symptom can vary across groups. Because no single level tells the whole story, the biopsychosocial model treats biology, psychology, and social context as interacting contributors. A useful companion idea is the diathesis-stress model: a predisposition, or diathesis, becomes disorder only when life stress is heavy enough to trigger it.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: The biopsychosocial model was articulated by the physician George Engel in 1977 as a corrective to purely biomedical thinking. Within psychology, Sigmund Freud founded the psychodynamic tradition. Behaviorism grew from the work of Ivan Pavlov on conditioned responses and B. F. Skinner on reinforcement, with John Watson promoting the approach in the United States. Joseph Wolpe applied learning principles to fear through systematic desensitization. The cognitive approach owes much to Aaron Beck, who linked depression to negative thinking patterns, and to Albert Ellis, whose rational emotive therapy challenged irrational beliefs. The humanistic approach is associated with Carl Rogers, who stressed unconditional positive regard, and Abraham Maslow, known for a hierarchy of needs. Sociocultural thinking draws on epidemiology and cross-cultural research showing that disadvantage, trauma, and social exclusion raise the risk of disorder. Together these contributors show why a single-cause story is usually too simple.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check your answers. 1) Which model emphasizes neurotransmitters and genes? 2) Which psychological school explains symptoms mainly through learning? 3) Who is most associated with the biopsychosocial model? 4) In the diathesis-stress model, what two ingredients combine to produce disorder? 5) Which approach would most likely recommend challenging distorted thoughts? Answers: 1) The biological model. 2) Behaviorism. 3) George Engel. 4) A predisposition or vulnerability (the diathesis) plus a sufficient amount of life stress. 5) The cognitive approach, associated with Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis, which targets the thinking patterns that sustain distress.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: A common mistake is treating the models as mutually exclusive, as if a disorder must be either biological or psychological. In practice they interact, and the biopsychosocial view holds them together. Another mistake is equating the biological model with the claim that medication is the only real treatment; therapy changes the brain too, and often works as well as or better than medication for many conditions. A third mistake is ignoring the social level, which can mean missing poverty, abuse, or discrimination that drives suffering. Exit ticket: (a) Name the three broad levels combined in the biopsychosocial model. (b) Give one treatment suggested by the cognitive approach. Answers: (a) Biological, psychological, and social. (b) Identifying and challenging distorted or unhelpful thoughts, as in cognitive therapy, to change the feelings and behaviors that follow from them.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to explain what a diagnostic classification system is for, describe the DSM-5 and how it relates to the ICD, and weigh the benefits and risks of putting a diagnostic label on a person. You will be able to distinguish a categorical approach, which sorts people into named disorders, from a dimensional approach, which rates symptoms along a scale. Warm-up from the diagnostic: what is the standard manual used to classify mental disorders in the United States? As you read, keep in mind that a diagnosis is a tool, not an identity. Used well, it helps clinicians communicate, choose treatments, and study outcomes. Used carelessly, it can reduce a person to a label. The goal is to use classification as a shared language while remembering the individual it describes.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A classification system gives clinicians a shared vocabulary so that the same term means roughly the same thing everywhere. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, now in its fifth edition (DSM-5), is published by the American Psychiatric Association and lists disorders with specific criteria, such as how many symptoms must be present and for how long. The World Health Organization publishes a parallel system, the International Classification of Diseases (ICD), used widely around the world. The DSM takes a mostly categorical approach: a person either meets the criteria for a disorder or does not. Critics note that real symptoms often vary by degree, so recent editions have added dimensional ratings in places. Good diagnosis improves communication, guides treatment, and supports research and insurance. The risks include overdiagnosis, cultural bias, and the stigma a label can carry, so criteria are meant to require genuine distress or impairment, not mere difference.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: The DSM has evolved across editions. The third edition, DSM-III, published in 1980 under the leadership of the psychiatrist Robert Spitzer, was a turning point: it introduced explicit, checklist-style criteria meant to make diagnosis more reliable across clinicians. The current DSM-5 appeared in 2013, and a text revision, the DSM-5-TR, followed in 2022 with updated wording and data. The World Health Organization's ICD, now in its eleventh revision (ICD-11), serves as the global standard and is broadly harmonized with the DSM. Reliability and validity are the two central aims of any such system: reliability means different clinicians reach the same diagnosis, and validity means the diagnosis genuinely tracks a real and useful distinction. Debates continue about where to draw lines, how to handle culture, and whether dimensional models better capture the continuous nature of many symptoms. These works show classification as an ongoing, self-correcting scientific project rather than a fixed list.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check your answers. 1) Who publishes the DSM-5? 2) Which organization publishes the ICD? 3) What is the difference between a categorical and a dimensional approach? 4) Name one benefit and one risk of diagnostic labeling. 5) What does it mean for a diagnostic system to be reliable? Answers: 1) The American Psychiatric Association. 2) The World Health Organization. 3) A categorical approach sorts people into discrete named disorders, while a dimensional approach rates symptoms along a continuum of severity. 4) Benefit: a shared language that guides treatment and research. Risk: stigma, overdiagnosis, or cultural bias from applying a label. 5) That different clinicians, assessing the same person, tend to arrive at the same diagnosis.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: A common mistake is treating the DSM as a finished, perfectly objective list rather than an evolving scientific document with genuine debates inside it. Another is confusing the DSM with the ICD; they are parallel, broadly aligned systems from different bodies. A third mistake is forgetting that the criteria require real distress or impairment, so that ordinary variation in personality or mood is not itself a disorder. Finally, avoid letting a diagnosis become the whole story of a person. Exit ticket: (a) Give the full name behind the abbreviation DSM. (b) Name the edition that introduced explicit checklist criteria and roughly when. Answers: (a) The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. (b) DSM-III, published in 1980, which introduced explicit, criteria-based definitions to improve reliability.

questions.prompt: The four Ds used to help judge abnormality are distress, dysfunction, danger, and...
questions.explanation: Deviance means behavior far outside cultural norms; the four are weighed together, not alone.

questions.prompt: Moral treatment, promoted at places like the York Retreat, replaced restraint with...
questions.explanation: Moral treatment emphasized humane, structured care over restraint.

questions.prompt: In the diathesis-stress model, a disorder appears when a predisposition meets...
questions.explanation: A vulnerability (diathesis) becomes disorder when stress is heavy enough to trigger it.

questions.prompt: The biopsychosocial model combines biological, psychological, and which third level?
questions.explanation: The social level includes family, culture, poverty, and discrimination.

questions.prompt: A categorical classification system differs from a dimensional one because it...
options: rates every symptom on a long scale
sorts people into discrete named disorders
questions.explanation: Categorical systems assign discrete diagnoses; dimensional systems rate severity along a continuum.

questions.prompt: The global classification system published by the World Health Organization is the...
questions.explanation: The ICD (International Classification of Diseases) is the WHO system, broadly aligned with the DSM.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to describe the main anxiety disorders, explain what distinguishes obsessive-compulsive disorder, and summarize how trauma can lead to post-traumatic stress disorder. You will be able to name the leading psychological treatments, especially those based on gradual exposure. Warm-up from the diagnostic: what are the two linked parts that define OCD? As you read, remember that anxiety itself is normal and even useful; it becomes a disorder only when it is excessive, persistent, and impairing. These conditions are among the most common mental disorders, and they are also among the most treatable, which is a genuinely hopeful fact. The compassionate point to hold onto is that avoidance feels protective in the short term but tends to keep fear alive, which is exactly why facing feared situations gradually and safely is so powerful.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Anxiety disorders involve excessive fear or worry that interferes with life. They include generalized anxiety disorder, marked by persistent, hard-to-control worry; panic disorder, with sudden surges of intense fear and physical symptoms; specific phobias, which are strong fears of particular objects or situations; and social anxiety disorder, a fear of judgment in social settings. Obsessive-compulsive disorder is now classified in its own chapter in the DSM-5. It pairs obsessions, which are unwanted intrusive thoughts, with compulsions, which are repetitive acts performed to reduce the anxiety those thoughts create. Trauma- and stressor-related disorders, also a separate chapter, include post-traumatic stress disorder, which can follow exposure to a terrifying event and features intrusive memories, avoidance, negative mood changes, and heightened arousal. Across these conditions, avoidance provides short-term relief but maintains the problem over time, which is why treatment so often works by carefully reversing avoidance.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT, is the best-supported psychological treatment for these conditions, and it draws on several traditions. Joseph Wolpe developed systematic desensitization, pairing relaxation with a gradual, step-by-step approach to feared situations. From this grew exposure therapy, and for OCD specifically, exposure and response prevention, in which a person faces triggers while resisting the compulsion until the anxiety subsides on its own. Aaron Beck's cognitive therapy added work on the beliefs that fuel fear, such as catastrophic predictions. For PTSD, trauma-focused CBT and prolonged exposure are well-established, and eye movement desensitization and reprocessing is also used. Medications, particularly a class of antidepressants known as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, can help and are often combined with therapy. The DSM-5 marked an important change by moving OCD and trauma-related disorders out of the anxiety chapter into chapters of their own, reflecting research on how they differ.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check your answers. 1) Which disorder features sudden surges of intense fear with strong physical symptoms? 2) Define an obsession and a compulsion. 3) What event type can precede PTSD? 4) Why does avoidance tend to keep anxiety going? 5) What does the response prevention part of treatment for OCD ask the person to do? Answers: 1) Panic disorder. 2) An obsession is an unwanted, intrusive thought or urge; a compulsion is a repetitive act done to reduce the distress the obsession causes. 3) Exposure to a terrifying or life-threatening event, such as an assault, accident, disaster, or combat. 4) Avoidance brings quick relief, which rewards the behavior and prevents the person from learning that the feared outcome is unlikely or manageable. 5) To resist performing the compulsion while facing the trigger, so anxiety can fall on its own.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: A common mistake is calling everyday nervousness a disorder; anxiety becomes a disorder only when it is excessive, lasting, and impairing. Another mistake is thinking OCD is just a taste for tidiness; true OCD involves distressing obsessions and compulsions that consume time and cause suffering. A third is assuming people with PTSD should simply avoid reminders; while compassion and safety come first, lasting recovery usually involves processing the memory with support rather than permanent avoidance. Exit ticket: (a) Name two anxiety disorders. (b) Name the exposure-based treatment used specifically for OCD. Answers: (a) For example, generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, specific phobia, or social anxiety disorder. (b) Exposure and response prevention, in which the person faces triggers while resisting compulsions.

lessons.title: Mood disorders, bipolar, and suicide risk

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to describe major depressive disorder and bipolar disorder, tell the difference between a depressive episode and a manic episode, and talk about suicide risk responsibly. You will be able to name common treatments for mood disorders. Warm-up from the diagnostic: what distinguishes bipolar disorder from depression that occurs on its own? This is a sensitive topic, and it deserves care. Depression is not weakness or laziness, and suicidal thoughts are a signal of pain, not a character flaw. The most important practical message is also the most hopeful one: these conditions are treatable, help exists, and asking someone directly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea. It opens a door to support. If you or someone you know is in crisis, contacting a local emergency number or a crisis line is the right first step.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Mood disorders involve disturbances in emotional state that are severe and lasting enough to impair life. Major depressive disorder features at least two weeks of low mood or loss of interest, along with symptoms such as changes in sleep, appetite, energy, and concentration, feelings of worthlessness, and sometimes thoughts of death. Bipolar disorder adds episodes at the other extreme: mania, a period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood with increased energy, reduced need for sleep, and risky behavior, or the milder hypomania. Bipolar I involves full manic episodes; bipolar II involves hypomania with depression. Suicide risk is raised across mood disorders and some other conditions, which is why clinicians assess it directly and compassionately. Warning signs can include hopelessness, talking about being a burden, giving away possessions, and withdrawal. Taking any such sign seriously, listening without judgment, and connecting the person to professional help can save a life.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Aaron Beck's cognitive theory of depression proposed that negative beliefs about the self, the world, and the future sustain low mood, and his cognitive therapy became a leading, well-tested treatment. Behavioral activation, which rebuilds engagement in rewarding activities, is also effective, as is interpersonal therapy, which focuses on relationships and life transitions. For medication, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors and related antidepressants are common first choices for depression. For bipolar disorder, mood stabilizers are central; lithium, whose use in mania was reported by the physician John Cade in 1949, remains an important treatment and has evidence for reducing suicide risk. In severe or treatment-resistant cases, electroconvulsive therapy, delivered under modern anesthesia, can be effective and life-saving. Crisis resources, including telephone and text lines, provide immediate support. These works together show that mood disorders respond to a range of treatments, often best in combination.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check your answers. 1) What is the minimum duration of low mood or lost interest for a depressive episode? 2) How does bipolar I differ from bipolar II? 3) Name one symptom of a manic episode. 4) Does asking someone directly about suicidal thoughts increase their risk? 5) Name one medication class used for bipolar disorder. Answers: 1) At least two weeks. 2) Bipolar I involves full manic episodes, while bipolar II involves hypomania (a milder high) together with depressive episodes. 3) For example, reduced need for sleep, racing thoughts, elevated or irritable mood, inflated self-esteem, or risky behavior. 4) No; asking directly and calmly does not plant the idea, and it opens the way to help. 5) Mood stabilizers, such as lithium.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: A common mistake is treating depression as ordinary sadness that willpower should fix; it is a medical condition with real biological and psychological features. Another mistake is confusing everyday mood swings with bipolar disorder, which involves distinct, sustained episodes that impair functioning. A third, and most important, is avoiding the subject of suicide out of fear; silence does not protect people, while honest, caring conversation and prompt professional help do. Never promise secrecy about safety. Exit ticket: (a) Name two symptoms of major depressive disorder beyond low mood. (b) State the responsible first response if someone tells you they are thinking of suicide. Answers: (a) For example, loss of interest, sleep or appetite changes, low energy, poor concentration, or feelings of worthlessness. (b) Stay with them, listen without judgment, and connect them to professional help or a crisis line or emergency number right away.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to describe schizophrenia and its positive and negative symptoms, outline the main groups of personality disorders, and summarize the key eating disorders and neurodevelopmental conditions. This is a wide survey, so aim for the big picture rather than every detail. Warm-up from the diagnostic: are hallucinations counted as positive or negative symptoms of schizophrenia? Throughout, a compassionate frame matters especially here, because these conditions are heavily stigmatized and often misunderstood. People with schizophrenia are far more likely to be victims of violence than perpetrators, and most live quiet lives, particularly with treatment and support. Personality disorders, eating disorders, and neurodevelopmental differences each call for understanding rather than blame. By the end you should be able to describe each category accurately and in language that respects the people it concerns.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Schizophrenia is a serious disorder affecting thought, perception, and emotion. Positive symptoms add experiences that are not shared by others, such as hallucinations and delusions; negative symptoms are reductions, such as flat emotional expression, reduced speech, and loss of motivation; and cognitive symptoms affect memory and attention. Personality disorders are enduring patterns of inner experience and behavior that differ markedly from cultural expectations and cause distress or impairment; they are often grouped into three clusters, commonly described as the odd or eccentric, the dramatic or erratic, and the anxious or fearful. Eating disorders include anorexia nervosa, marked by restriction and intense fear of weight gain; bulimia nervosa, marked by binge eating followed by compensatory behavior; and binge-eating disorder. Neurodevelopmental disorders begin in early development and include autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and intellectual disability. These are differences in how the brain develops, not failures of effort.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: The study of schizophrenia owes much to Emil Kraepelin, who described a pattern he called dementia praecox, and to Eugen Bleuler, who introduced the term schizophrenia to capture a splitting of mental functions, not a split personality. Treatment advanced with the first antipsychotic medications in the 1950s, which target positive symptoms, alongside psychosocial support, family education, and rehabilitation. For personality disorders, Marsha Linehan developed dialectical behavior therapy, which has strong evidence for borderline personality disorder and for reducing self-harm. Eating disorders are treated with specialized psychotherapies, family-based treatment for younger patients, and careful medical monitoring, since anorexia nervosa carries serious physical risks. For neurodevelopmental conditions, early support, education, and accommodations help people thrive; attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder also responds to behavioral strategies and, in many cases, medication. Across all of these, the modern emphasis is on realistic hope, support, and respect for the person.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check your answers. 1) Give one positive and one negative symptom of schizophrenia. 2) Who introduced the term schizophrenia? 3) What distinguishes anorexia nervosa from bulimia nervosa? 4) Name two neurodevelopmental disorders. 5) Which therapy is strongly linked with treating borderline personality disorder? Answers: 1) Positive: a hallucination or delusion. Negative: flat affect, reduced speech, or loss of motivation. 2) Eugen Bleuler. 3) Anorexia nervosa centers on restriction and low body weight with intense fear of weight gain, while bulimia nervosa involves cycles of binge eating followed by compensatory behavior such as purging. 4) For example, autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, or intellectual disability. 5) Dialectical behavior therapy, developed by Marsha Linehan.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: A common mistake is confusing schizophrenia with split or multiple personalities; the word refers to disruptions in thought and perception, not two identities. Another mistake is believing people with schizophrenia are inherently dangerous; most are not, and they are more often harmed than harmful. A third is treating eating disorders as vanity or a lifestyle choice rather than serious illnesses with real medical risk, and a fourth is seeing neurodevelopmental differences as laziness rather than differences in development. Exit ticket: (a) Name the two broad symptom groups in schizophrenia. (b) Name the three commonly described clusters of personality disorders. Answers: (a) Positive symptoms (added experiences such as hallucinations and delusions) and negative symptoms (reductions such as flat affect and low motivation). (b) The odd or eccentric, the dramatic or erratic, and the anxious or fearful.

lessons.title: Approaches to treatment and reducing stigma

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to summarize the main approaches to treating mental disorders - psychotherapy, medication, and their combination - and explain why reducing stigma is itself part of good care. You will be able to name several major therapies and medication classes and match them to broad uses. Warm-up from the diagnostic: which statement about mental illness is best supported by evidence? This closing lesson ties the course together. The central, hopeful theme is that mental disorders are common and that many respond well to treatment, especially when people can seek help without shame. Stigma is not a harmless attitude; it delays care, deepens isolation, and worsens outcomes. Learning to speak and think accurately about mental illness is therefore not just good manners but a genuine contribution to public health and to the dignity of people who live with these conditions.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Treatment generally draws on two broad tools used alone or together. Psychotherapy, or talking therapy, includes cognitive behavioral therapy, which targets thoughts and behaviors; psychodynamic therapy, which explores patterns rooted in past experience; and humanistic or person-centered therapy, which supports growth and self-acceptance. Medication works on the body and brain and includes antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, and anti-anxiety drugs. For many conditions, the combination of therapy and medication outperforms either alone. Beyond the clinic, support from family, peers, and community services, along with lifestyle factors such as sleep, exercise, and connection, all contribute to recovery. Reducing stigma is a crucial part of the picture, because shame and fear keep people from seeking care. Accurate information, respectful and person-first language, and contact with people who have lived experience all reduce stigma and help people get help earlier, when treatment tends to work best.

sections.heading: Key figures & works
sections.text: Cognitive behavioral therapy grew from the cognitive work of Aaron Beck and the behavioral tradition of researchers such as B. F. Skinner and Joseph Wolpe, and it is now among the most studied and widely used therapies. Carl Rogers developed person-centered therapy, emphasizing empathy and unconditional positive regard. In medication, the first antipsychotics in the 1950s transformed the care of psychosis, antidepressants such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors became common from the late 20th century, and lithium, reported by John Cade in 1949, remains central for bipolar disorder. On the stigma side, research on contact-based education shows that meeting and hearing from people with lived experience reduces prejudice more effectively than facts alone, and movements for person-first language and open conversation have shifted public attitudes. Together these works support a practical conclusion: effective treatments exist, and a less stigmatizing culture helps people reach them.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check your answers. 1) Name two broad categories of treatment for mental disorders. 2) For many conditions, what often works better than therapy or medication alone? 3) Name one medication class and a condition it is commonly used for. 4) Why does stigma harm health and not just feelings? 5) What kind of education is especially effective at reducing stigma? Answers: 1) Psychotherapy and medication. 2) The combination of psychotherapy and medication together. 3) For example, antidepressants for depression, antipsychotics for schizophrenia, or mood stabilizers for bipolar disorder. 4) Stigma creates shame and fear that delay or prevent people from seeking care, which worsens outcomes and deepens isolation. 5) Contact-based education, in which people meet and hear from those with lived experience of mental illness.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: A common mistake is assuming medication is always necessary or always the answer; for many conditions therapy is as effective, and the best plan is tailored to the person. Another mistake is viewing therapy as merely venting; evidence-based therapies are structured, skill-building treatments. A third is underestimating stigma, treating it as a matter of politeness rather than a real barrier to care. Finally, avoid defining people by their diagnosis; prefer person-first language. Exit ticket: (a) Name one evidence-based psychotherapy and what it works on. (b) Give one concrete way to reduce stigma in everyday life. Answers: (a) For example, cognitive behavioral therapy, which changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviors to reduce distress. (b) Use accurate, person-first language, speak openly and without judgment about mental health, and encourage people to seek help early.
